claim: chinmo is expressed during embryogenesis and early larval development and is strongly downregulated from L3
source: Examination of chinmo expression revealed that it is expressed during embryogenesis and early larval development and that it is strongly downregulated from L3 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A measuring chinmo mRNA levels across developmental stages

claim: Chinmo protein is present in L1 and L2 stages and disappears in late L3 in imaginal and larval tissues
source: Immunostaining analysis in imaginal and larval tissues confirmed the presence of Chinmo in L1 and L2 stages and its disappearance in late L3 (Figure 1B and C), an expression profile that is in agreement with previous studies (Narbonne-Reveau and Maurange, 2019; Truman and Riddiford, 2022).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1B and C, and corroborated by citations to previous studies

claim: chinmo-depleted animals show developmental arrest at the end of the first instar larval stage presenting a tanned cuticle reminiscent of the puparium
source: chinmo-depleted animals showed developmental arrest at the end of the first instar larval stage presenting a tanned cuticle clearly reminiscent of the tanned larval cuticle of the puparium (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic observation shown in Figure 1D of Act-Gal4 driven chinmoRNAi larvae

claim: Arrested chinmo-depleted larvae precociously express pupal cuticle genes while blocking larval-specific genes activation
source: Consistent with the phenotype, we found that arrested chinmo-depleted larvae precociously expressed pupal cuticle genes while blocked larval-specific genes activation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1E showing upregulation of Edg78E and downregulation of Crp47Eg, Lcp65Ag3, and CG30457

claim: chinmo is required for normal progression of the organism during the larval period
source: These results confirm that chinmo is required for normal progression of the organism during the larval period, as proposed by Truman and Riddiford, 2022.
evidence: Inferred from the developmental arrest phenotype and gene expression changes, with citation to supporting work

claim: Depletion of chinmo in salivary glands causes a dramatic decrease in normal larval development with strong reduction in size and DNA content of gland cells
source: As it is shown in Figure 2A, although depletion of chinmo in the salivary glands did not affect the formation of this organ, it caused a dramatic decrease in normal larval development, as revealed by the strong reduction in size and DNA content of the gland cells (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements in Figure 2B-D showing reduced salivary gland size, DAPI intensity, and nuclear size

claim: Expression levels of early and late specific salivary gland protein encoding genes (ng1-3 and Sgs) are virtually undetectable in chinmo-depleted salivary glands
source: Consistently, the expression levels of both early and late specific salivary gland protein encoding genes, such as new glue 1–3 (ng) and Salivary gland secretion (Sgs), were virtually undetectable in chinmo-depleted salivary glands compared to control (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2E showing dramatic reduction in ng1-3 and Sgs gene expression

claim: Depletion of chinmo in tracheal cells results in reduction in nuclear size and DNA content of tracheal cells as well as reduced length of the organ
source: Although depletion of chinmo specifically in the tracheal cells, using a trh-Gal4 driver, resulted in many arrested L2 larvae with a necrotic tracheal system, escapers that reached L3 presented reduction in nuclear size and DNA content of tracheal cells as well as reduced length of the organ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), thus confirming that Chinmo is required for proper growth of larval tissues.
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 of tracheal cell size, DAPI intensity, and tracheal length

claim: Chinmo is required for proper growth of larval tissues
source: Although depletion of chinmo specifically in the tracheal cells, using a trh-Gal4 driver, resulted in many arrested L2 larvae with a necrotic tracheal system, escapers that reached L3 presented reduction in nuclear size and DNA content of tracheal cells as well as reduced length of the organ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), thus confirming that Chinmo is required for proper growth of larval tissues.
evidence: Inferred from multiple observations of growth defects in salivary glands and trachea upon chinmo depletion

claim: Depletion of chinmo in the wing pouch strongly impedes larval development, with the wing pouch being strongly reduced and not showing expression of patterning genes wg and ct
source: Thus, in late L3 wing discs only the notum, which does not express the esg-Gal4 driver, was observed while the wing pouch, revealed by positive GFP signal, was strongly reduced and did not show the expression of patterning genes such as wingless (wg) and cut (ct) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 3A showing absence of Wg and Ct expression in chinmo-depleted wing pouches

claim: Most chinmo-depleted animals arrest development as pharate adults, and escapers that eclose (15%) have no wings
source: In line with these results, although most of the chinmo-depleted animals arrested development as pharate adults, escapers that were able to eclose (15%) had no wings (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by adult phenotype images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing wingless flies

claim: Depletion of chinmo in the eye disc abolishes the developing tissue and the formation of the adult eye
source: Similarly, depletion of chinmo in the eye disc using a specific driver (ey-Gal4) induced similar effects abolishing the developing tissue and the formation of the adult eye (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing reduced eye disc and eyeless adult flies

claim: Chinmo is required during the larval period to control the development and function of larval and imaginal tissues
source: Taken together, these data show that Chinmo is required during the larval period to control the development and function of larval and imaginal tissues.
evidence: Inferred from multiple tissue-specific depletion experiments showing developmental defects in both larval and imaginal tissues

claim: Both salivary glands and wing discs show a significant and premature increase of Br-C protein levels as early as in L1 larvae upon chinmo depletion
source: Contrary to recently published data (Truman and Riddiford, 2022), both tissues showed a significant and premature increase of Br-C protein levels as early as in L1 larvae, while no increase in E93 protein levels was detected in any tissue (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 4 showing Br-C upregulation in chinmo-depleted tissues, and contradicts a previous publication

claim: No increase in E93 protein levels is detected in salivary glands or wing discs upon chinmo depletion
source: Contrary to recently published data (Truman and Riddiford, 2022), both tissues showed a significant and premature increase of Br-C protein levels as early as in L1 larvae, while no increase in E93 protein levels was detected in any tissue (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 4 showing no E93 upregulation in chinmo-depleted tissues

claim: Ectopic expression of Br-CZ1 blocks Chinmo activation
source: As previously described, ectopic expression of Br-CZ1 blocked Chinmo activation (Narbonne-Reveau and Maurange, 2019).
evidence: Observation supported by citation to previous work

claim: Precocious upregulation of Br-C blocks development in both salivary glands and wing discs, phenocopying the loss of function of chinmo
source: As a consequence, precocious upregulation of Br-C blocked development in both tissues, phenocopying the loss of function of chinmo (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing growth defects upon Br-CZ1 overexpression

claim: A fundamental function of Chinmo is to suppress the expression of the pupal specifier Br-C during the juvenile stages
source: This result suggests that a fundamental function of Chinmo is to suppress the expression of the pupal specifier Br-C during the juvenile stages.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Br-C overexpression phenocopies chinmo loss of function

claim: Salivary glands show the same growth impairment upon simultaneous depletion of chinmo and Br-C as observed upon chinmo depletion alone
source: Remarkably, whereas salivary glands showed the same growth impairment observed upon chinmo depletion (Figure 5A-F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), depletion of Br-C largely rescued the abnormalities in the wing discs caused by depletion of chinmo
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 5A-F showing no rescue of salivary gland size, DNA content, or gene expression in double knockdown

claim: Depletion of Br-C largely rescues the abnormalities in wing discs caused by depletion of chinmo
source: Remarkably, whereas salivary glands showed the same growth impairment observed upon chinmo depletion (Figure 5A-F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), depletion of Br-C largely rescued the abnormalities in the wing discs caused by depletion of chinmo: the double knock-out wing discs developed in a regular manner to reach normal size by the end of L3 and showed proper expression of patterning genes such as wg (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 5G showing normal wing disc development and Wg expression in double knockdown

claim: Depletion of Br-C in the eye disc rescues the phenotype induced by the absence of chinmo
source: Whereas depletion of Br-C in the eye disc rescued the phenotype induced by the absence of chinmo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the larval trachea failed to restore the growth defects observed in chinmo-depleted tracheal cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing rescue of eye disc development in double knockdown

claim: The larval trachea fails to restore the growth defects observed in chinmo-depleted tracheal cells upon Br-C depletion
source: Whereas depletion of Br-C in the eye disc rescued the phenotype induced by the absence of chinmo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the larval trachea failed to restore the growth defects observed in chinmo-depleted tracheal cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing no rescue of tracheal growth defects in double knockdown

claim: A major regulatory function of chinmo during early larval development in imaginal cells is channelled through the repression of Br-C
source: Taken together, our results suggest that a major regulatory function of chinmo during early larval development in imaginal cells is channelled through the repression of Br-C, while in larval tissues chinmo appears to exert specific growth-related functions that are independent to Br-C repression.
evidence: Inferred from the differential rescue of wing disc versus salivary gland phenotypes upon Br-C co-depletion

claim: In larval tissues chinmo exerts specific growth-related functions that are independent of Br-C repression
source: Taken together, our results suggest that a major regulatory function of chinmo during early larval development in imaginal cells is channelled through the repression of Br-C, while in larval tissues chinmo appears to exert specific growth-related functions that are independent to Br-C repression.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of rescue of salivary gland and tracheal phenotypes upon Br-C co-depletion

claim: In imaginal cells chinmo ensures the expression of juvenile genes by repressing Br-C, a well-known inhibitor of larval gene expression
source: Thus, in the imaginal cells chinmo appears to ensure the expression of juvenile genes by repressing Br-C, a well-known inhibitor of larval gene expression (Zhou and Riddiford, 2002).
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of imaginal disc phenotypes and supported by citation to Br-C function

claim: Br-C might repress the early expression of critical components of signaling pathways such as Wg and EGFR involved in wing fate specification in early larval development
source: In this regard, it is tempting to speculate that Br-C might repress the early expression of critical components of signaling pathways such as Wg and EGFR, involved in wing fate specification in early larval development (Ng et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2000; Zecca and Struhl, 2002).
evidence: Speculative statement based on observed loss of Wg expression and supported by citations to pathway functions

claim: In larval tissues chinmo exerts an active role promoting growth and maturation
source: In contrast, in larval tissues chinmo seems to exert an active role promoting growth and maturation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Br-C-dependent Sgs genes fail to activate in absence of chinmo despite premature Br-C expression

claim: The Br-C-dependent Sgs genes fail to be activated in absence of chinmo when Br-C is prematurely expressed
source: The fact that the Br-C-dependent Sgs genes fail to be activated in absence of chinmo, when Br-C is prematurely expressed, supports this idea (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2E showing lack of Sgs expression in chinmo-depleted salivary glands

claim: Br-C is necessary for the degeneration of the larval salivary glands during the onset of the pupal period
source: Thus, while Br-C is necessary for the degeneration of the larval salivary glands during the onset of the pupal period (Jiang et al., 2000), it is critical for the correct eversion of the imaginal wing disc and for the temporary G2 arrest that synchronises the cell cycle in the wing epithelium during early pupa wing elongation (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Br-C is critical for the correct eversion of the imaginal wing disc and for the temporary G2 arrest that synchronises the cell cycle in the wing epithelium during early pupa wing elongation
source: Thus, while Br-C is necessary for the degeneration of the larval salivary glands during the onset of the pupal period (Jiang et al., 2000), it is critical for the correct eversion of the imaginal wing disc and for the temporary G2 arrest that synchronises the cell cycle in the wing epithelium during early pupa wing elongation (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: E93 is necessary to activate autophagy for elimination of the larval mushroom body neuroblasts in late pupae
source: Likewise, E93 is necessary to activate autophagy for elimination of the larval mushroom body neuroblasts in late pupae (Pahl et al., 2019), whereas it controls the terminal adult differentiation of the imaginal wing during the same period (Ureña et al., 2016; Uyehara et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: E93 controls the terminal adult differentiation of the imaginal wing during late pupal period
source: Likewise, E93 is necessary to activate autophagy for elimination of the larval mushroom body neuroblasts in late pupae (Pahl et al., 2019), whereas it controls the terminal adult differentiation of the imaginal wing during the same period (Ureña et al., 2016; Uyehara et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Overexpression of chinmo from early L3 in the anterior compartment of the wing disc impairs its larva-pupal transition by abolishing Br-C expression and inducing apoptosis at late L3
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, overexpression of chinmo from early L3 in the anterior compartment of the disc using the cubitus interruptus ci-Gal4 driver impaired its larva-pupal transition as abolished Br-C expression and induced apoptosis at late L3 as revealed by the high expression of the effector caspase Dcp-1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 6A showing loss of Br-C and high Dcp-1 expression

claim: Overexpression of chinmo results in dramatically reduced size of the anterior compartment and halted expression of patterning genes such as ct
source: As a result, the size of the anterior compartment was dramatically reduced, and the expression of patterning genes such as ct was halted (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 6B showing loss of Ct expression

claim: Impairment of ct expression upon chinmo overexpression is not just a consequence of cell death but a distinct response to sustained chinmo expression or consequent Br-C depletion
source: Impairment of ct expression was not just a consequence of cell death, as ct expression was neither detected in wing discs overexpressing both chinmo and the p35 inhibitor of effector caspases (Hay et al., 1994; Figure 6C and D), but instead to a distinct response to the sustained expression of chinmo or to the consequent depletion of Br-C.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6C-D showing loss of Ct despite blocking apoptosis with p35

claim: Depletion of Br-C in the anterior compartment of the wing disc results in high Chinmo levels, strong Dcp-1 staining, and impairment of ct expression
source: Therefore, we knocked down Br-C in the anterior compartment of the wing disc and confirmed that Chinmo levels remained high in this compartment by late L3. Also, in this case we observed a strong Dcp-1 staining and impairment of ct expression (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 6E-F showing maintained Chinmo, high Dcp-1, and loss of Ct

claim: Simultaneous depletion of chinmo and Br-C from early L3 does not lead to an increase in apoptosis nor altered expression of patterning genes
source: Importantly, simultaneous depletion of chinmo and Br-C from early L3 did not lead to an increase in apoptosis (Figure 6G) nor altered the expression of patterning genes (Figure 5F), which indicates that tissue death at the end of the larval period is due to sustained expression of chinmo rather than the absence of Br-C.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 6G showing no Dcp-1 and Figure 5F showing normal Wg expression in double knockdown

claim: Tissue death at the end of the larval period is due to sustained expression of chinmo rather than the absence of Br-C
source: Importantly, simultaneous depletion of chinmo and Br-C from early L3 did not lead to an increase in apoptosis (Figure 6G) nor altered the expression of patterning genes (Figure 5F), which indicates that tissue death at the end of the larval period is due to sustained expression of chinmo rather than the absence of Br-C.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of apoptosis in double knockdown experiments

claim: The transition from larva to pupa must take place in the absence of the larval specifier Chinmo
source: Altogether, these results confirm that the transition from larva to pupa must take place in the absence of the larval specifier Chinmo.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that sustained chinmo expression blocks the larva-pupa transition

claim: Ectopic expression of chinmo during the pupal stage leads to a marked decrease in E93 protein levels
source: To that aim, larvae were maintained at 18°C until 12 hr after pupa formation (APF) and then shifted to 29°C to allow the Gal4 to function. The resulting ectopic expression of chinmo led to a marked decrease in E93 protein levels (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7A showing reduced E93 upon chinmo overexpression

claim: Ectopic expression of chinmo during pupal stage results in strongly undifferentiated anterior compartment of the wing, reminiscent of E93-depleted wings
source: As a result, the anterior compartment of the wing was strongly undifferentiated, a phenotype reminiscent of that observed in E93-depleted wings (Ureña et al., 2016; Ureña et al., 2014; Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by cuticle preparation in Figure 7B showing undifferentiated wing and citation to E93 depletion phenotype

claim: chinmo must be downregulated during the initiation and throughout the metamorphic transition to allow the sequential expression of the pupal specifier Br-C and the adult specifier E93
source: Taken together, our results show that chinmo must be downregulated during the initiation and throughout the metamorphic transition to allow the sequential expression of the pupal specifier Br-C and the adult specifier E93.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that sustained chinmo expression blocks both Br-C and E93 function

claim: Overexpression of Drosophila chinmo has been found to cooperate with Ras or Notch to trigger massive tumour overgrowth
source: However, while overexpression of Drosophila chinmo has been found to cooperate with Ras or Notch to trigger massive tumour overgrowth (Doggett et al., 2015), changes in Drosophila Br-C expression have not been associated with any effect on tumourigenesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Changes in Drosophila Br-C expression have not been associated with any effect on tumourigenesis
source: However, while overexpression of Drosophila chinmo has been found to cooperate with Ras or Notch to trigger massive tumour overgrowth (Doggett et al., 2015), changes in Drosophila Br-C expression have not been associated with any effect on tumourigenesis.
evidence: Statement about absence of previous findings in the literature

claim: RNAi-mediated depletion of Br-C in wing discs in the downregulated lgl background results in an increase in the mean wing pouch volume compared to downregulation of lgl alone
source: Interestingly, RNAi-mediated depletion of Br-C in the wing discs in the downregulated lgl background resulted in an increase in the mean wing pouch volume compared to the downregulation of lgl alone (Figure 8B, C and G).
evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification data in Figure 8G showing increased pouch volume

claim: Overexpression of Br-C in the lgl background reduces the size of the lgl-induced overgrowth, confirming that Br-C expression elicits tumour suppressor activity
source: Consistently, overexpression of Br-C in the same lgl background had the opposite effect, reducing the size of the lgl-induced overgrowth, thereby confirming that Br-C expression elicits tumour suppressor activity (Figure 8D and G).
evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification data in Figure 8G showing decreased pouch volume

claim: Overexpression of E93 reduces the size of lgl overgrowth
source: We found that overexpression of E93 also reduced the size of lgl overgrowth (Figure 8E and G).
evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification data in Figure 8G showing decreased pouch volume

claim: Combined overexpression of E93 with the p35 inhibitor of apoptosis still leads to a reduction in the size of the wing pouch in the lgl-sensitised background
source: However, combined overexpression of E93 with the p35 inhibitor of apoptosis still lead to a reduction in the size of the wing pouch in the lgl-sensitised background (Figure 8F and G).
evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification data in Figure 8G showing decreased pouch volume despite blocking apoptosis

claim: chinmo and Br-C/E93 play opposite functions, chinmo with pro-oncogenic features and Br-C and E93 acting as tumour suppressor genes
source: Thus, also in this regard, chinmo and Br-C/E93 play opposite functions, chinmo with pro-oncogenic features and Br-C and E93 act as tumour suppressor genes.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects on tumor growth in lgl background

claim: A chinmo orthologue (Bg-chinmo) is present in the Blattella germanica genome
source: A detailed Tblastn search in the Blattella genome database revealed the presence of a chinmo orthologue (Bg-chinmo).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic search results

claim: Bg-chinmo is highly expressed in embryos and decreases dramatically thereafter during nymphal development
source: We found that it is highly expressed in embryos and decreases dramatically thereafter during nymphal development (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 9A showing Bg-chinmo expression across developmental stages

claim: 43% of Bg-chinmoRNAi animals undergo only one nymphal molt before molting to an early adult after the N5 stage
source: Importantly, whereas Control larvae underwent two nymphal molts before initiating metamorphosis at the end of the N6 stage, 43% of Bg-chinmoRNAi animals underwent only one nymphal molt before molting to an early adult after the N5 stage (Figure 9B–E).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 9B-E

claim: Precocious Bg-chinmo-depleted adults are smaller than control counterparts as they skip a nymphal stage
source: Precocious Bg-chinmo-depleted adults were smaller than control counterparts as they skipped a nymphal stage.
evidence: Supported by size measurements in Figure 9E

claim: Precocious Bg-chinmo-depleted adults present all the external characteristics of an adult, including functional hind- and fore-wings, adult legs, adult cerci, mature genitalia, and adult-specific cuticle pigmentation
source: However, they presented all the external characteristics of an adult, namely functional hind- and fore-wings, adult legs (Figure 9F), adult cerci, mature genitalia, and adult-specific cuticle pigmentation.
evidence: Supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 9C-F

claim: The role of Chinmo as juvenile specifier seems to be conserved in hemimetabolous insects, indicating that its developmental function precedes the hemimetabolous-holometabolous split
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the role of Chinmo as juvenile specifier seems to be conserved in hemimetabolous insects, thereby indicating that its developmental function precedes the hemimetabolous-holometabolous split.
evidence: Inferred from the precocious metamorphosis phenotype in Blattella upon Bg-chinmo depletion

claim: The temporal expression of Chinmo, Br-C, and E93 determines the tissue acquisition of gradual differentiation features from the juvenile to the adult to generate the distinct organs
source: In summary, we identified Chinmo as a new member of the metamorphic gene network acting as a general larval specifier, as recently proposed by Truman and Riddiford, 2022. Together with a number of previous reports (reviewed in Martín et al., 2021), our results show that the temporal expression of Chinmo, Br-C, and E93 determines the tissue acquisition of gradual differentiation features from the juvenile to the adult to generate the distinct organs.
evidence: Inferred from all experimental results and supported by citations to previous work

claim: Chinmo maintains cells in an undifferentiated state, whereas Br-C and E93 induce progressively the differentiation program
source: Whereas Chinmo maintains cells in an undifferentiated state, Br-C and E93 induce progressively the differentiation program.
evidence: Inferred from the functional characterization of these factors throughout the manuscript

claim: The chinmo-to-Br-C transition in Drosophila has been associated with the loss of the regenerative potential of imaginal cells
source: Similarly, the chinmo-to-Br-C transition in Drosophila has been associated with the loss of the regenerative potential of imaginal cells (Narbonne-Reveau and Maurange, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The fact that Br-C and E93 act as a tumour suppressor in an overproliferative background supports the idea that they induce differentiation
source: The fact that Br-C and E93 act as a tumour suppressor in an overproliferative background supports this idea.
evidence: Inferred from the tumor suppressor experiments with lgl background

claim: The role of chinmo as larval specifier is conserved in hemimetabolous insects
source: Finally, we found that the role of chinmo as larval specifier is conserved in hemimetabolous insects.
evidence: Supported by the Blattella experiments showing precocious metamorphosis

claim: In hemimetabolous insects, the transition from juvenile to adult relies mainly on the shift from Chinmo to E93 during the last nymphal stage, with Kr-h1 also involved in preventing metamorphosis through the repression of E93
source: Since hemimetabolous insects do not undergo the intermediate pupal stage, the transition from juvenile to adult, therefore, relies mainly on the shift from Chinmo to E93 during the last nymphal stage, with Kr-h1 also involved in preventing metamorphosis through the repression of E93 (Ureña et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from the absence of pupal stage in hemimetabolans and supported by citation

claim: In hemimetabolous insects, depletion of Br-C does not impair metamorphosis
source: However, although in hemimetabolans insects depletion of Br-C does not impair metamorphosis, Br-C does regulate the progressive growth of the metamorphic tissues, such as the wing pads and the dorsal thorax (Erezyilmaz et al., 2006; Fernandez-Nicolas et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2013; Konopova et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Br-C regulates the progressive growth of the metamorphic tissues, such as the wing pads and the dorsal thorax in hemimetabolous insects
source: However, although in hemimetabolans insects depletion of Br-C does not impair metamorphosis, Br-C does regulate the progressive growth of the metamorphic tissues, such as the wing pads and the dorsal thorax (Erezyilmaz et al., 2006; Fernandez-Nicolas et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2013; Konopova et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: A premetamorphic role of Br-C was already present in hemimetabolous insects, acquiring an additional metamorphic role as pupal specifier during the evolution of holometabolous insects
source: This observation suggests that a premetamorphic role of Br-C was already present in hemimetabolous insects, acquiring an additional metamorphic role as pupal specifier during the evolution of holometabolous insects.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Br-C regulates growth but not metamorphosis in hemimetabolans

claim: The deployment of the pupal-specific genetic program is controlled by the expression of Br-C at the larval-pupal transition
source: The deployment of the pupal-specific genetic program is controlled by the expression of Br-C at the larval-pupal transition (Truman, 2019; Zhou and Riddiford, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Upon the formation of the pupa, hormone signalling triggers the expression of E93, whose product represses Br-C expression and directs the formation of the final differentiated adult structures
source: Upon the formation of the pupa, hormone signalling triggers the expression of the helix-turn-helix factor E93, whose product represses Br-C expression and directs the formation of the final differentiated adult structures (Chafino et al., 2019; Martín et al., 2021; Ureña et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Br-C and E93 are the stage-specifying genes for the pupal and adult states
source: While it is firmly established that Br-C and E93 are the stage-specifying genes for the pupal and adult states, the nature of the larval specifying gene has been elusive.
evidence: Statement of established scientific consensus

claim: Larval identity has been attributed to Kr-h1, which is present during the larval period and represses Br-C and E93 expression during this period
source: To date, larval identity has been attributed to Kr-h1, which is present during the larval period and represses Br-C and E93 expression during this period (Huang et al., 2011; Ureña et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Kr-h1 is critical for maintaining the larval state
source: However, although Kr-h1 is undoubtedly critical for maintaining the larval state, evidence has shown that this factor cannot be considered the larval specifier per se.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge

claim: Depletion of Kr-h1 in Drosophila does not prevent normal larval development nor a timely transition to the pupa
source: For example, depletion of Kr-h1 in Drosophila does not prevent normal larval development nor a timely transition to the pupa (Beck et al., 2004; Pecasse et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The product of chronologically inappropriate morphogenesis (chinmo) gene has been recently proposed to be responsible for larval identity in Drosophila
source: In this regard, the product of chronologically inappropriate morphogenesis (chinmo) gene, another member of the BTB family of transcription factors, has been recently proposed to be responsible for larval identity in Drosophila (Truman and Riddiford, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study

claim: Chinmo was first isolated based on its requirement for the temporal identity of mushroom body neurons
source: First isolated based on its requirement for the temporal identity of mushroom body neurons (Zhu et al., 2006), the identification of Chinmo as a more general larval specifier has provided invaluable insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the control of juvenile identity.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: In humans, many BTB-zinc finger transcription factors have been implicated in cancer, where they have opposing effects, from oncogenic to tumour suppressor functions
source: In humans, many such factors have been implicated in cancer, where they have opposing effects, from oncogenic to tumour suppressor functions (Siggs and Beutler, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Early-born neurons in the central nervous system are characterised by the expression of Chinmo, whereas smaller late-born neurons are marked by expression of Br-C
source: This effect has already been shown in the central nervous system where early-born neurons are characterised by the expression of Chinmo, whereas smaller late-born neurons are marked by expression of Br-C (Maurange et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study
